chapters.title: Preamble
paragraphs: A spectre is haunting Europe—the spectre of communism. All the powers of old Europe have entered into a holy alliance to exorcise this spectre: Pope and Czar, Metternich and Guizot, French radicals and German police-spies.

Where is the opposition party that has not been smeared as communist by its rivals in power? Where is the opposition that has not flung the same branding charge of communism back—at the more advanced opposition parties as well as at its reactionary enemies?
Two things follow from this fact.
I. Communism is already acknowledged by all the European powers to be itself a power.

II. It is high time that communists openly, in the face of the whole world, publish their views, their aims, their tendencies, and answer this nursery tale of the Spectre of Communism with a manifesto of the party itself.
To this end, communists of various nationalities have assembled in London and drafted the following Manifesto, to be published in the English, French, German, Italian, Flemish, and Danish languages.

chapters.title: I. Bourgeois and Proletarians
paragraphs: The history of every society that has existed until now is a history of struggles between classes.

Free man and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman—in short, oppressor and oppressed—were constantly set against each other. Their struggle never stopped, sometimes hidden and sometimes open, and each time it ended either in the revolutionary reconstruction of society as a whole or in the shared destruction of the classes fighting it out.

In earlier periods of history, almost everywhere we find society arranged in a complicated series of orders, with many different levels of social rank. Ancient Rome had patricians, knights, plebeians, and slaves; the Middle Ages had feudal lords, vassals, guild-masters, journeymen, apprentices, and serfs. Within nearly all these classes there were further divisions of rank.

Modern bourgeois society, which grew out of feudal society’s ruins, has not abolished the antagonisms between classes. It has simply replaced the old classes with new ones, the old conditions of oppression with new conditions, and the old forms of struggle with new forms. Our age—the age of the bourgeoisie—does, however, have one distinguishing feature: it has made these class antagonisms simpler. More and more, the whole of society is dividing into two great enemy camps, two great classes confronting each other directly: Bourgeoisie and Proletariat.
The chartered burghers of the earliest towns emerged from the serfs of the Middle Ages. These burgesses in turn provided the first elements from which the bourgeoisie developed.

America’s discovery and the voyage around the Cape opened new territory for the rising bourgeoisie. Markets in the East Indies and China, the colonisation of America, commerce with the colonies, the growth in the means of exchange and in commodities generally—all gave trade, navigation, and industry a stimulus without precedent. In this way they rapidly strengthened the revolutionary element within the crumbling society of feudalism.

The feudal organisation of industry, in which closed guilds held a monopoly over industrial production, could no longer meet the expanding needs of the new markets. Manufacture replaced it. The manufacturing middle class pushed the guild-masters aside; the division of labour between separate corporate guilds gave way to a division of labour inside each individual workshop.

Meanwhile, markets went on expanding and demand kept rising. Even manufacture could no longer meet the need. Steam power and machinery then transformed industrial production. The giant of Modern Industry displaced manufacture, and industrial millionaires—the commanders of entire industrial armies, the modern bourgeois—displaced the industrial middle class.

Modern Industry created the world market that America’s discovery had prepared the way for. That market brought enormous growth in trade, navigation, and transport and communication by land. In turn, this growth stimulated the further expansion of industry. As industry, trade, navigation, and railways spread, the bourgeoisie grew with them, enlarged its capital, and drove every class inherited from the Middle Ages into the background.
We can therefore see that the modern bourgeoisie itself emerged through a long process of development, through a succession of revolutions in the modes of production and exchange.

Every stage in the bourgeoisie’s development brought a corresponding advance in its political position. Under the feudal nobility it was an oppressed class; in the medieval commune it became an armed association governing itself. In some places it formed independent urban republics, as in Italy and Germany; elsewhere it formed the monarchy’s taxable “third estate,” as in France. Later, during the period of manufacture proper, it served the semi-feudal or absolute monarchy as a counterweight to the nobility, and indeed as a cornerstone of the great monarchies generally. Finally, with the rise of Modern Industry and the world market, the bourgeoisie won exclusive political power in the modern representative State. The executive of that State is merely a committee administering the shared affairs of the bourgeoisie as a whole.
Throughout history, the bourgeoisie has played a profoundly revolutionary role.

Wherever the bourgeoisie has gained power, it has brought all feudal, patriarchal, and idyllic relationships to an end. It has ruthlessly ripped apart the varied feudal bonds tying people to their “natural superiors,” leaving no connection between one person and another except naked self-interest and the cold transaction of “cash payment.” It has submerged the loftiest ecstasies of religious devotion, chivalric enthusiasm, and philistine sentiment in the freezing water of selfish calculation. It has turned personal worth into exchange value. In place of countless chartered freedoms that could never be taken away, it has installed one unscrupulous freedom: Free Trade. In short, it has replaced exploitation hidden behind religious and political illusions with exploitation that is naked, shameless, direct, and brutal.

The bourgeoisie has torn the halo from every occupation once honoured and regarded with reverent awe. It has turned the physician, lawyer, priest, poet, and man of science into wage labourers in its pay.
The bourgeoisie has ripped the sentimental covering from the family, turning relations within it into nothing more than relations of money.

The bourgeoisie has revealed how the brutal displays of energy in the Middle Ages, so admired by Reactionists, were fittingly complemented by utter sloth and idleness. It was the first to demonstrate what human activity can achieve. Its wonders have far outdone the Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, and Gothic cathedrals; its expeditions have eclipsed every earlier Exodus of nations and every crusade.

The bourgeoisie can survive only by continually revolutionising the instruments of production, and therefore the relations of production, and with them the entire network of social relations. For all earlier industrial classes, by contrast, survival first required the preservation of the old modes of production unchanged. What sets the bourgeois age apart from every earlier age is the continual transformation of production, the ceaseless disruption of every social condition, perpetual uncertainty and unrest. Every settled, frozen relationship, together with its following of ancient, revered prejudices and beliefs, is swept aside. Every newly formed relationship grows outdated before it has time to harden. Everything solid dissolves into air; everything holy is desecrated; and at last people are forced to look clear-eyed at the actual conditions of their lives and their relations with their fellow human beings.
The need for an ever larger market for its products drives the bourgeoisie across the entire globe. Everywhere it must find a foothold, everywhere settle, everywhere establish connections.

By exploiting the world market, the bourgeoisie has made production and consumption cosmopolitan in every country. To the bitter distress of Reactionists, it has pulled the national foundations out from beneath industry’s feet. Long-established national industries have either been destroyed already or are being destroyed each day. New industries push them out, and introducing these industries becomes a matter of life and death for every civilised nation. They process raw materials brought from the most distant regions instead of materials native to their own country, and their products are consumed not just at home but in every corner of the world. Old needs, once met by the country’s own production, give way to new needs that require products from distant lands and climates. The former isolation and self-sufficiency of localities and nations give way to contact in every direction and the universal interdependence of nations. What happens in material production happens in intellectual production too. The intellectual achievements of particular nations become everyone’s common property. National narrowness and one-sidedness grow increasingly impossible, and a world literature emerges from the many national and local literatures.

Through the rapid improvement of every instrument of production and the vastly easier means of communication, the bourgeoisie pulls all nations, even the most barbarian, into civilisation. Its cheap commodities are the heavy artillery that demolishes every Chinese wall and forces the barbarians’ fiercely stubborn hatred of foreigners to surrender. It makes every nation adopt the bourgeois mode of production on pain of extinction. It forces them to bring what it calls civilisation into their own midst—that is, to become bourgeois themselves. In short, it fashions a world in its own image.

The bourgeoisie has placed the countryside under the towns’ control. It has built enormous cities and greatly enlarged the urban population in proportion to the rural, thus rescuing a considerable share of the population from the idiocy of rural life. As it has made the countryside depend on the towns, so it has made barbarian and semi-barbarian countries depend on civilised countries, peasant nations on bourgeois nations, and the East on the West.

The bourgeoisie increasingly puts an end to the dispersal of population, means of production, and property. It has gathered production together and concentrated property in a few hands. Political centralisation necessarily followed. Provinces that were independent or only loosely linked, with their own interests, laws, governments, and tax systems, were bundled into a single nation: one government, one legal code, one national class interest, one frontier, and one customs tariff. In barely a hundred years of rule, the bourgeoisie has brought into being productive forces more immense and colossal than those of all earlier generations combined. The harnessing of Nature’s forces by human beings, machinery, chemistry applied to industry and agriculture, steam navigation, railways, electric telegraphs, entire continents cleared for cultivation, rivers made into canals, whole populations conjured from the ground—what earlier century so much as suspected that such productive forces lay asleep in the lap of social labour?

We can see, then, that the means of production and exchange on which the bourgeoisie built itself up originated inside feudal society. At a certain point in their development, those means no longer fitted the conditions under which feudal society produced and exchanged: its feudal organisation of agriculture and manufacture, or, in a word, its feudal property relations. These relations had become incompatible with the productive forces already developed; they had turned into chains. Those chains had to be shattered, and shattered they were.
Free competition took their place, together with a social and political constitution suited to it and the economic and political domination of the bourgeois class.

A comparable process is taking place before our eyes. Modern bourgeois society, with its relations of production, exchange, and property, has summoned up such gigantic means of production and exchange that it resembles a sorcerer unable to control the powers of the underworld called forth by his spells. For decades now, the history of industry and trade has been a history of modern productive forces rebelling against modern conditions of production, against the property relations on which the bourgeoisie’s existence and rule depend. We need only mention the commercial crises whose periodic return challenges the very existence of the whole of bourgeois society, more menacingly each time. In these crises, a large part not only of existing products but also of the productive forces previously created is repeatedly destroyed. An epidemic breaks out that would have seemed absurd in every earlier age: the epidemic of overproduction. Society suddenly finds itself thrown back into temporary barbarism. It seems as though famine or a universal war of devastation has severed every supply of the necessities of life; industry and trade seem annihilated. And why? Because there is too much civilisation, too much provision for subsistence, too much industry, too much trade. Society’s productive forces no longer help the conditions of bourgeois property develop. On the contrary, they have grown too powerful for those conditions, which hold them in chains. As soon as they break these chains, they throw the whole of bourgeois society into disorder and threaten the existence of bourgeois property. The conditions of bourgeois society are too confined to contain the wealth they have created. How, then, does the bourgeoisie overcome these crises? On one side, by forcibly destroying a mass of productive forces; on the other, by conquering fresh markets and exploiting existing ones more intensively. In other words, it prepares still wider and more destructive crises while reducing the means of preventing them.
The weapons the bourgeoisie used to strike feudalism down are now directed against the bourgeoisie itself.
But the bourgeoisie has done more than forge the weapons that will kill it: it has also brought into being the people who will wield them—the modern working class, the proletarians.

As the bourgeoisie—that is, capital—develops, the proletariat, the modern working class, develops at the same rate. This is a class of labourers who can live only while they find work, and can find work only while their labour adds to capital. Forced to sell themselves a piece at a time, these labourers are commodities like any other article traded, and are therefore subject to every turn of competition and every fluctuation in the market.

The widespread use of machinery and the division of labour have stripped proletarian work of its individual character and, with that, of all its attraction for the worker. He becomes an attachment to the machine, required to perform only the simplest, most repetitive knack, the one easiest to learn. As a result, the cost of producing a worker is almost entirely limited to the necessities that keep him alive and allow his race to reproduce. But a commodity’s price—and therefore the price of labour as well—is equal to its production cost. So the more repellent the work becomes, the lower the wage falls. More than that: as machinery and the division of labour spread, the burden of work also grows in the same proportion, whether through longer working hours, more work demanded within a given time, faster machinery, and so on.

Modern Industry has transformed the patriarchal master’s small workshop into the industrial capitalist’s vast factory. Workers crowded together in the factory are organised as soldiers. These rank-and-file troops of the industrial army answer to a complete hierarchy of officers and sergeants. They are slaves not only to the bourgeois class and the bourgeois State: day after day, hour after hour, they are enslaved by the machine, by the overseer, and above all by the individual bourgeois manufacturer himself. The more openly this tyranny announces that profit is its purpose and goal, the pettier, more hateful, and more embittering it becomes.

The less skill and physical effort manual labour requires—in other words, the further Modern Industry develops—the more women’s labour replaces men’s. For the working class, distinctions of age and sex lose any separate social significance. All are instruments of labour, costing more or less to use according to their age and sex.

The moment the manufacturer’s exploitation of the worker reaches the point where his wages are paid in cash, other sections of the bourgeoisie descend on him: the landlord, the shopkeeper, the pawnbroker, and the rest.

The lower layers of the middle class—small tradespeople, shopkeepers, retired tradesmen generally, craftsmen, and peasants—gradually sink into the proletariat. In part, this is because their small capital cannot support the scale of Modern Industry and is overwhelmed in competition with the great capitalists; in part, it is because new methods of production make their specialised skill worthless. In this way the proletariat draws its recruits from every class of the population.

The proletariat develops through several stages. Its struggle against the bourgeoisie begins as soon as it comes into being. At first individual workers fight, then the workers in a single factory, then those in one trade in one locality, against the particular bourgeois who directly exploits them. Their attacks target the instruments of production themselves rather than the bourgeois conditions of production. They destroy imported goods competing with their labour, smash machinery to pieces, and set factories on fire. They try to recover by force the vanished position of the medieval worker.

At this point the workers still make up a disconnected mass, scattered across the country and divided by competition with each other. Where they gather into more cohesive bodies, this is not yet the result of their own active union. It comes from the bourgeoisie’s unity: to achieve its political aims, that class must mobilise the entire proletariat, and for a time it still has the power to do so. At this stage, then, proletarians fight their enemies’ enemies rather than their own: the remnants of absolute monarchy, the landowners, the non-industrial bourgeois, and the petty bourgeoisie. The whole movement of history is thus concentrated in the bourgeoisie’s hands, and every victory won in this way belongs to the bourgeoisie.

As industry develops, however, the proletariat not only grows in number but is gathered together in larger masses. Its strength increases, and it becomes more aware of that strength. The differing interests and living conditions within its ranks become steadily more alike, as machinery erases distinctions between kinds of labour and almost everywhere brings wages down to the same low level. Intensifying competition among the bourgeois, and the commercial crises it produces, make workers’ wages fluctuate ever more sharply. Continual improvements in machinery, developing at an ever faster pace, make their livelihoods increasingly insecure. Conflicts between individual workers and individual bourgeois increasingly become conflicts between two classes. Workers then start forming combinations—Trades Unions—against the bourgeois. They join forces to maintain wage rates and create permanent associations to prepare for these occasional revolts. Here and there, the conflict erupts into riots.

Workers sometimes win, but their victories last only a while. The true fruit of their struggles is the workers’ steadily expanding union, rather than the immediate outcome. Modern Industry helps that union by creating better means of communication, bringing workers in different places into contact with one another. This contact was precisely what was needed to draw the many local struggles, all alike in character, into one national class struggle. Every class struggle, however, is a political struggle. The union that took the medieval burghers centuries to achieve, with their wretched roads, takes modern proletarians only a few years, thanks to the railways.

Competition among workers themselves continually disrupts this organisation of proletarians into a class and therefore into a political party. Yet it rises again each time, stronger, more solid, and more powerful. Exploiting divisions within the bourgeoisie, it forces particular workers’ interests to be recognised in law. This is how England’s ten-hours’ bill was passed.

Taken together, conflicts between the classes of the old society advance the proletariat’s development in many ways. The bourgeoisie finds itself continually at war: first against the aristocracy, later against those parts of its own class whose interests obstruct industrial progress, and always against the bourgeoisie of other countries. In each of these struggles it must appeal to the proletariat for help, drawing it into the political arena. The bourgeoisie itself thus provides the proletariat with the means of political and general education—in other words, it gives the proletariat weapons to turn against the bourgeoisie.

Furthermore, as we have already seen, industrial progress throws whole sections of the ruling classes into the proletariat, or at least threatens the conditions of their existence. These sections too bring the proletariat new sources of enlightenment and progress.

Finally, as the class struggle approaches its decisive moment, the disintegration within the ruling class—and indeed throughout the whole of society—becomes so violent and unmistakable that a small part of that ruling class breaks away and joins the revolutionary class, the class that holds the future in its hands. Just as part of the nobility once crossed over to the bourgeoisie, so part of the bourgeoisie now crosses over to the proletariat. This is particularly true of some bourgeois ideologists who have reached a theoretical understanding of the historical movement as a whole.

Of all the classes confronting the bourgeoisie today, only the proletariat is truly revolutionary. Modern Industry makes the other classes decay and ultimately disappear; the proletariat is its distinctive and indispensable product. The lower middle class—the small manufacturer, shopkeeper, artisan, and peasant—fights the bourgeoisie to preserve its existence as parts of the middle class. These people are therefore conservative, not revolutionary. More than that, they are reactionary, because they try to turn history’s wheel backwards. If they do happen to act in a revolutionary way, it is only because they face an imminent descent into the proletariat. In that case they defend their future interests rather than their present ones, abandoning their own standpoint for the proletariat’s.

The “dangerous class,” that social scum, that passively decaying mass cast off by the lowest layers of the old society, may here and there be swept into a proletarian revolution. Its conditions of life, however, make it far more suited to serving as a paid instrument of reactionary intrigue.

The conditions of the proletariat have already almost submerged those of the old society as a whole. The proletarian owns no property; his relations with his wife and children no longer have anything in common with bourgeois family relations. Modern industrial labour and modern subjection to capital, alike in England and France, America and Germany, have stripped away every trace of his national character. To him, law, morality, and religion are simply bourgeois prejudices, with corresponding bourgeois interests lying in ambush behind them.

Every earlier class that gained power tried to secure its newly acquired position by making society as a whole conform to its own conditions of appropriation. Proletarians can take command of society’s productive forces only by abolishing their own former mode of appropriation, and with it every other previously existing mode. They have nothing of their own to protect and strengthen. Their task is to destroy every earlier safeguard and guarantee of individual property.

All earlier movements in history were movements of minorities or served minority interests. The proletarian movement is the independent, self-conscious movement of the overwhelming majority, serving that overwhelming majority’s interests. The proletariat, the lowest layer of our present society, cannot move or lift itself up without blasting into the air all the layers of official society piled above it.

At first the proletariat’s struggle against the bourgeoisie takes a national form, though its substance is not national. Naturally, the proletariat in each country must first settle accounts with the bourgeoisie of its own country.

In outlining the broadest stages of the proletariat’s development, we have followed the more or less concealed civil war raging within present society to the point where it erupts into open revolution, and where the violent overthrow of the bourgeoisie establishes the basis for proletarian rule.

As we have seen, every previous form of society rested on the antagonism between oppressing and oppressed classes. But to oppress a class, one must guarantee it at least the conditions that let it continue its slavish existence. Under serfdom, the serf rose to become a member of the commune, just as the petty bourgeois, beneath the yoke of feudal absolutism, managed to become a bourgeois. By contrast, the modern labourer does not rise as industry advances: he falls further and further beneath even his own class’s conditions of existence. He becomes a pauper, and pauperism grows faster than population and wealth. At this point it becomes clear that the bourgeoisie is no longer fit to rule society or impose its conditions of existence as society’s overriding law. It is unfit because it cannot guarantee its slave a living even within slavery, because it cannot prevent him from sinking to a condition where it must feed him instead of being fed by him. Society can no longer live under this bourgeoisie; in other words, the bourgeoisie’s continued existence has become incompatible with society.

The essential condition of the bourgeois class’s existence and rule is the creation and growth of capital, and capital depends on wage-labour. Wage-labour depends entirely on competition among labourers. Industrial progress, which the bourgeoisie promotes without intending its consequences, replaces the workers’ isolation through competition with their revolutionary union through association. The development of Modern Industry therefore pulls from beneath the bourgeoisie’s feet the very foundation on which it produces and appropriates products. Above all, the bourgeoisie produces its own grave-diggers. Its downfall and the proletariat’s victory are equally unavoidable.

chapters.title: II. Proletarians and Communists
paragraphs: How do the Communists relate to the proletariat taken as a whole?
The Communists are not a separate party standing against the other parties of the working class.
They have no interests of their own distinct from the interests of the proletariat as a whole.
They put forward no sectarian principles of their own to serve as a mould for the proletarian movement.

Only two things distinguish the Communists from other working-class parties. (1) In the national struggles waged by proletarians in different countries, they identify and foreground the shared interests of the entire proletariat, regardless of nationality. (2) Through every stage that the working class’s struggle against the bourgeoisie must pass, they represent, at every time and in every place, the interests of the movement as a whole.

In practical terms, then, the Communists are the most advanced and determined section of the working-class parties in every country, the section that drives all the others forward. In theoretical terms, their advantage over the great mass of the proletariat is a clear understanding of the proletarian movement’s direction, the conditions under which it advances, and its ultimate overall results.

The Communist’s immediate objective is shared by all the other proletarian parties: to organise the proletariat into a class, overthrow bourgeois supremacy, and win political power for the proletariat.

Communist theoretical conclusions do not rest in any way on ideas or principles invented or discovered by one or another self-appointed reformer of the world. They simply express in general terms the actual relations arising from a class struggle already under way, from a historical movement taking place before our eyes. Abolishing existing property relations is by no means unique to Communism.
Throughout the past, every form of property relations has continually changed as the historical conditions on which it rests have changed.
For instance, the French Revolution did away with feudal property and replaced it with bourgeois property.

What distinguishes Communism is the abolition of bourgeois property, rather than property in general. Modern bourgeois private property, however, is the final and fullest expression of a system for producing and appropriating products founded on antagonisms between classes, on the few exploiting the many.
Understood in this sense, Communist theory can be stated in a single sentence: the abolition of private property.

We Communists are accused of wanting to abolish a person’s right to acquire property as the fruit of his own labour—property supposedly forming the foundation of every individual’s freedom, activity, and independence.

Property won through hard work, acquired by oneself, earned by oneself! Are you talking about the small artisan’s or small peasant’s property, which existed before bourgeois property? There is no need for us to abolish it: industrial development has already destroyed much of it and continues destroying it every day.
Or is it modern bourgeois private property that you mean?

But does wage-labour give the labourer any property? None at all. It produces capital: property that exploits wage-labour and can grow only by bringing forth a fresh supply of wage-labour to exploit anew. Property in its present form rests on the antagonism between capital and wage-labour. Let us look at each side of that antagonism.

Being a capitalist means occupying a social _status_ in production, not merely a personal one. Capital is collectively produced. It can be put to work only through the combined action of many members of society—indeed, ultimately, through the combined action of all society’s members.
Capital, then, is a power belonging to society, rather than a personal power.

Turning capital into common property, the property of all society’s members, therefore does not turn personal property into social property. What changes is only the property’s social character: it ceases to have a class character.
Now let us turn to wage-labour.

The average price paid for wage-labour is the minimum wage: the quantity of necessities absolutely required to keep a labourer barely alive. What the wage-labourer appropriates through his work is therefore just enough to sustain and reproduce a bare existence. We have no intention of abolishing this personal appropriation of labour’s products, which maintains and reproduces human life without leaving a surplus that could be used to command someone else’s labour. We want to abolish only the wretched character of this appropriation, under which the worker lives solely to enlarge capital and is permitted to live only as far as the ruling class’s interests require.
In bourgeois society, living labour serves merely to enlarge accumulated labour. In Communist society, accumulated labour serves merely to broaden, enrich, and advance the worker’s life.

So in bourgeois society the past rules the present, while in Communist society the present rules the past. Under bourgeois society, capital has independence and individuality; the living person, meanwhile, is dependent and without individuality.

And the bourgeois calls the abolition of these conditions the abolition of individuality and freedom! Quite rightly. We certainly aim to abolish bourgeois individuality, bourgeois independence, and bourgeois freedom.
Under today’s bourgeois conditions of production, freedom means free trade: the freedom to buy and to sell.

But once buying and selling disappear, the freedom to buy and sell disappears with them. All this talk of free buying and selling, and all the bourgeoisie’s other “brave words” about freedom generally, have meaning, if they have any at all, only when contrasted with restricted buying and selling and the shackled traders of the Middle Ages. They mean nothing as an objection to Communism’s abolition of buying and selling, of bourgeois conditions of production, and of the bourgeoisie itself.

Our intention to abolish private property fills you with horror. Yet in your existing society, nine-tenths of the population already have no private property. The few possess it only because those nine-tenths do not. You therefore accuse us of wanting to abolish a form of property that can exist only on the condition that the overwhelming majority of society has no property at all.
In short, you accuse us of intending to abolish your property. Exactly: that is precisely what we intend to do.

You say individuality disappears the moment labour can no longer be turned into capital, money, or rent—into a social power that can be monopolised. That is, it disappears the moment individual property can no longer become bourgeois property, can no longer become capital.
You must therefore admit that by “individual” you mean only the bourgeois, the middle-class property owner, and no one else. That person must indeed be cleared out of the way and made impossible.
Communism takes away no one’s ability to appropriate society’s products. It takes away only the ability to use that appropriation to bring other people’s labour under his control.
The objection has been raised that abolishing private property will put a stop to all work and engulf us in universal laziness.

By that reasoning, bourgeois society should have collapsed into ruin from sheer idleness long ago: its members who work acquire nothing, and those who acquire anything do no work. The entire objection simply restates the tautology that wage-labour cannot continue to exist once capital has ceased to exist.

Every objection made to the Communist way of producing and appropriating material products has likewise been made to its ways of producing and appropriating intellectual products. To the bourgeois, the end of class property means the end of production itself; in just the same way, the end of class culture means to him the end of culture altogether.
For the vast majority, the culture whose loss he mourns amounts to nothing more than training to function as a machine.

But do not argue with us while judging our proposed abolition of bourgeois property by your bourgeois ideas of freedom, culture, law, and so forth. Those very ideas grow out of the conditions of bourgeois production and bourgeois property. Your jurisprudence is likewise nothing but your class’s will turned into a law for everyone—a will whose basic character and direction are determined by the economic conditions of your class’s existence.

You share with every earlier ruling class a self-serving misconception: you turn the social forms arising from your present mode of production and form of property into eternal laws of nature and reason. Yet these are historical relations that emerge and disappear as production develops. What you clearly recognise about ancient property, and acknowledge about feudal property, you are naturally forbidden to acknowledge about your own bourgeois form of property.
Abolish the family! Even the most radical people fly into a rage at this notorious Communist proposal.

What is the foundation of today’s family, the bourgeois family? Capital and private profit. This family exists in its fully developed form only within the bourgeoisie. Its counterpart, however, is the family’s practical absence among proletarians, together with public prostitution.
The bourgeois family will naturally disappear when its counterpart disappears, and both will disappear when capital itself is gone.
Do you accuse us of wanting to end parents’ exploitation of their children? We plead guilty to that crime.
But, you will object, we destroy the most sacred relationships by replacing education at home with education by society.

And what about your education! Is it not social too, shaped by the social conditions in which you educate and by society’s direct or indirect intervention through schools and other means? The Communists did not invent society’s intervention in education. They seek only to change its character and free education from the ruling class’s influence.

Bourgeois nonsense about family and education, about the sacred bond between parent and child, grows all the more revolting as Modern Industry tears apart every family tie among proletarians and turns their children into mere commodities and instruments of labour.
But you Communists want to introduce community of women, the entire bourgeoisie screams together.

The bourgeois regards his wife as nothing more than an instrument of production. He hears that instruments of production are to be used in common and naturally reaches the only conclusion he can: women too must be destined to become common to everyone.
He does not even suspect that the actual purpose is to end women’s position as mere instruments of production.

Besides, nothing could be more ridiculous than our bourgeois gentlemen’s virtuous outrage over the community of women that they claim the Communists would openly and officially establish. Communists have no need to introduce community of women: it has existed from almost as far back as memory reaches.

Our bourgeois gentlemen are not satisfied with having proletarians’ wives and daughters at their disposal, quite apart from common prostitutes. They take the keenest pleasure in seducing one another’s wives as well.

Bourgeois marriage is actually a system of wives held in common. At most, therefore, the Communists might be accused of wanting to replace a hypocritically hidden community of women with one openly recognised by law. Beyond that, it is obvious that abolishing the present system of production must also abolish the community of women arising from it—that is, prostitution in both its public and private forms.
Communists are also accused of wanting to do away with countries and nationality.

Working men possess no country. We cannot take away what they do not have. The proletariat must first win political supremacy, become the nation’s leading class, and constitute itself as _the_ nation. To that extent it is itself national, although not in the bourgeois meaning of that word.

Differences and antagonisms between nations are disappearing more and more each day as the bourgeoisie develops, trade becomes free, the world market expands, and both the mode of production and its corresponding living conditions become uniform.
Proletarian supremacy will make them disappear still faster. Joint action by at least the leading civilised countries is among the first requirements for the proletariat’s emancipation.

As the exploitation of one individual by another is ended, the exploitation of one nation by another will also end. As the antagonism between classes inside a nation disappears, so will the hostility between that nation and other nations.
Accusations against Communism based on religion, philosophy, or an ideological standpoint in general do not deserve to be examined seriously.

Does it take profound insight to understand that human ideas, views, and conceptions—in short, human consciousness—change with every change in the conditions of material existence, in social relationships, and in social life?

What does the history of ideas demonstrate, if not that intellectual production changes its character as material production changes? In every age, the dominant ideas have been the ideas of the dominant class.

When people talk of ideas that revolutionise society, they are merely stating that the elements of a new society have developed within the old one, and that the disintegration of old ideas keeps pace with the disintegration of the old conditions of life.

As the ancient world entered its final agony, Christianity overcame the ancient religions. When Christian ideas gave way to rationalist ideas in the eighteenth century, feudal society was fighting its last battle against the bourgeoisie, then a revolutionary force. Ideas of religious liberty and freedom of conscience merely expressed free competition’s rule within the sphere of knowledge.

“Undoubtedly,” it will be said, “religious, moral, philosophical and juridical ideas have been modified in the course of historical development. But religion, morality philosophy, political science, and law, constantly survived this change.”

“There are, besides, eternal truths, such as Freedom, Justice, etc. that are common to all states of society. But Communism abolishes eternal truths, it abolishes all religion, and all morality, instead of constituting them on a new basis; it therefore acts in contradiction to all past historical experience.”
What does this accusation really amount to? All past society’s history has unfolded through the development of class antagonisms, taking different forms in different historical periods.

Whatever forms those antagonisms have taken, every past age shares one fact: one part of society exploits another. It is therefore no surprise that, despite all its multiplicity and variety, the social consciousness of past ages operates within certain common forms or general ideas. These can disappear completely only when class antagonisms disappear altogether.

The Communist revolution breaks with traditional property relations more radically than any other revolution. It is hardly surprising that, as it develops, it also breaks most radically with traditional ideas.
But let us put these bourgeois objections to Communism behind us.
We have already seen that the working-class revolution’s first step is to raise the proletariat to the ruling position, to win the battle for democracy.

The proletariat will use its political supremacy to take all capital from the bourgeoisie step by step, to concentrate every instrument of production in the hands of the State—that is, the proletariat organised as the ruling class—and to expand the total productive forces as quickly as possible.

Naturally, at first this can be achieved only through despotic attacks on property rights and the conditions of bourgeois production. It therefore requires measures that seem economically inadequate and unsustainable, but that, as the movement develops, reach beyond themselves and make further attacks on the old social order necessary. Such measures are unavoidable if the mode of production is to be revolutionised completely.
Naturally, the measures taken will vary from country to country.
Still, the following measures will be broadly applicable in the most advanced countries.
1. Abolish property in land and use every rent from land for purposes that serve the public.
2. Impose a heavy income tax on a progressive or graduated scale.
3. Abolish every right to receive an inheritance.
4. Confiscate all property belonging to emigrants and rebels.
5. Concentrate credit in the State’s hands through a national bank operating with State capital and holding an exclusive monopoly.
6. Place the means of communication and transport under the State’s centralised control.
7. Expand State-owned factories and instruments of production; bring waste-lands into cultivation and improve the soil more generally, carrying out these measures according to a shared plan.
8. Require everyone equally to work. Create industrial armies, with particular emphasis on agriculture.
9. Bring agriculture and manufacturing industries together; gradually remove the distinction between town and country by distributing the population more evenly across the country as a whole.
10. Provide free education in public schools for every child. Abolish children’s factory labour as it exists today. Combine education with industrial production, and so on, and so on.

Once development has removed class distinctions and concentrated all production in the hands of a vast association embracing the whole nation, public power will cease to be political in character. Political power, strictly understood, is simply one class’s organised power to oppress another. If circumstances force the proletariat, during its struggle against the bourgeoisie, to organise itself as a class; if revolution makes it the ruling class; and if, as ruler, it forcibly sweeps away the old conditions of production, then it will also sweep away the conditions that allow class antagonisms and classes themselves to exist. In doing so, it will abolish its own supremacy as a class.
The old bourgeois society, with its classes and the antagonisms between them, will give way to an association where each person’s free development is the condition of everyone’s free development.

chapters.title: III. Socialist and Communist Literature
paragraphs: 1. REACTIONARY SOCIALISM
_A. Feudal Socialism_

Their historical position made the aristocracies of France and England take up the task of writing pamphlets against modern bourgeois society. In France’s revolution of July 1830 and England’s agitation for reform, they once again fell before the detested upstart. After that, a serious political struggle was completely out of the question. Only a battle in literature remained possible. Yet even there, the old rallying cries of the restoration period could no longer be used.

To win sympathy, the aristocracy had to appear to set aside its own interests and frame its case against the bourgeoisie solely in the interests of the exploited working class. It thus took revenge by singing satirical songs about its new master and whispering grim predictions of approaching catastrophe into his ear.

This gave rise to Feudal Socialism: half a lament, half a lampoon; half an echo from the past, half a threat from the future. Its bitter, witty, cutting criticism sometimes struck the bourgeoisie straight to the heart. Yet its effect was always ridiculous, because it was utterly unable to understand the course of modern history.

To rally the people behind it, the aristocracy waved the proletarian’s begging bag as its banner. But whenever the people joined it, they spotted the old feudal coats of arms on its backside and walked away, laughing loudly and without respect.
Part of the French Legitimists, along with “Young England,” put on precisely this spectacle.

When the feudalists point out that their way of exploiting people differed from the bourgeoisie’s, they forget that the circumstances and conditions of their exploitation were entirely different and are now obsolete. When they show that the modern proletariat never existed under their rule, they forget that the modern bourgeoisie necessarily grew out of their own kind of society.

Besides, they barely conceal the reactionary nature of their criticism. Their chief accusation against the bourgeoisie amounts to this: under the bourgeois _regime_, a class is developing that is destined to tear the old order of society out by its roots.
What they blame the bourgeoisie for is less the creation of a proletariat than the creation of a _revolutionary_ proletariat.

In political practice, they therefore support every coercive measure directed against the working class. In everyday life, despite their grandiose phrases, they bend down to gather the golden apples fallen from industry’s tree, exchanging truth, love, and honour for business in wool, beetroot sugar, and potato spirits.
Just as the parson has always walked hand in hand with the landlord, Clerical Socialism has walked alongside Feudal Socialism.

Nothing could be easier than colouring Christian asceticism with Socialism. Has Christianity not denounced private property, marriage, and the State? Has it not preached charity and poverty in their place, celibacy and the mortification of the flesh, the monastic life and Mother Church? Christian Socialism is merely the holy water a priest uses to bless the aristocrat’s bitter resentment.
_B. Petty-Bourgeois Socialism_

The feudal aristocracy was not the only class the bourgeoisie ruined, nor the only one whose conditions of existence withered and died in modern bourgeois society’s atmosphere. The medieval burgesses and the small peasant landowners came before the modern bourgeoisie. In countries where industry and trade remain little developed, these two classes still linger in a vegetative existence alongside the rising bourgeoisie.

Where modern civilisation is fully developed, a new petty-bourgeois class has emerged, shifting between proletariat and bourgeoisie and continually renewing itself as an additional component of bourgeois society. Competition, however, constantly throws individual members of this class down into the proletariat. As Modern Industry advances, they even see the approaching moment when they will disappear altogether as an independent section of modern society, replaced in manufacture, agriculture, and trade by overseers, bailiffs, and shop assistants.

In countries such as France, where peasants make up well over half the population, writers who supported the proletariat against the bourgeoisie naturally judged the bourgeois _regime_ by peasant and petty-bourgeois standards. They defended the working class from the standpoint of these intermediate classes. This was the origin of petty-bourgeois Socialism. Sismondi led this school in England as well as in France.

This Socialist school analysed the contradictions within modern production’s conditions with great sharpness. It exposed economists’ hypocritical defences of the system. It demonstrated beyond dispute the disastrous consequences of machinery and the division of labour, the concentration of capital and land in a few hands, overproduction, and crises. It identified the unavoidable ruin of the petty bourgeois and peasant, proletarian misery, anarchy in production, glaring inequalities in the distribution of wealth, the industrial war of extermination among nations, and the dissolution of old moral bonds, old family relationships, and old nationalities.

In its positive programme, however, this Socialism aims either to restore the old means of production and exchange, along with the old property relations and old society, or to force modern means of production and exchange into the narrow frame of old property relations—relations these very means have already shattered and were bound to shatter. Whichever course it takes, it is both reactionary and Utopian.
Its final message is this: corporate guilds in manufacture and patriarchal relationships in agriculture.
In the end, when stubborn historical facts had dispelled self-deception’s intoxicating effects, this kind of Socialism collapsed into a wretched bout of the blues.
_C. German, or “True,” Socialism_

French Socialist and Communist literature arose under the pressure of a bourgeoisie already in power and expressed the struggle against that power. It arrived in Germany at a time when the German bourgeoisie had only just begun to struggle against feudal absolutism.

German philosophers, aspiring philosophers, and _beaux esprits_ seized eagerly on this literature. They forgot only one thing: when the writings crossed from France into Germany, France’s social conditions did not cross with them. In Germany’s social setting, the French literature lost all its immediate practical meaning and became purely literary. Thus eighteenth-century German philosophers saw the demands of the first French Revolution as nothing more than demands of “Practical Reason” in general. To them, the revolutionary French bourgeoisie’s expression of its will signified the law of pure Will, of Will as it ought to be, of true human Will in general.

The world of the German _literati_ consisted entirely of reconciling these new French ideas with their old philosophical conscience—or, more precisely, of annexing the French ideas while holding on to their own philosophical standpoint.
They annexed the ideas just as one takes possession of a foreign language: by translating them.

Everyone knows how monks wrote foolish lives of Catholic Saints _over_ manuscripts containing the classical works of pagan antiquity. With secular French literature, the German _literati_ did the reverse: they wrote their philosophical nonsense underneath the French original. Under the French critique of money’s economic functions, for example, they wrote “Alienation of Humanity”; under the French critique of the bourgeois State, they wrote “dethronement of the Category of the General,” and so on.

They called this insertion of philosophical phrases behind French historical criticism “Philosophy of Action,” “True Socialism,” “German Science of Socialism,” “Philosophical Foundation of Socialism,” and similar names.

French Socialist and Communist literature was thereby completely emasculated. Since, in German hands, it no longer expressed one class’s struggle against another, the German felt he had overcome “French one-sidedness.” He believed he represented the requirements of truth rather than true requirements, the interests of Human Nature rather than those of the proletariat: the interests of Man in general, who belongs to no class and has no reality, existing only in the hazy domain of philosophical fantasy.
Meanwhile, this German Socialism, so solemn and earnest about its schoolboy assignment, and so boastful in hawking its meagre wares like a charlatan, gradually shed its pedantic innocence.
The German bourgeoisie’s struggle, especially in Prussia, against feudal aristocracy and absolute monarchy—in other words, the liberal movement—became more serious.

This gave “True” Socialism the opportunity it had long wanted: to confront the political movement with Socialist demands; to hurl the customary curses at liberalism, representative government, bourgeois competition, bourgeois freedom of the press, bourgeois legislation, and bourgeois liberty and equality; and to preach to the masses that this bourgeois movement offered them nothing to gain and everything to lose. At just the right moment, German Socialism forgot that the French criticism it so foolishly echoed presupposed an already existing modern bourgeois society, with its corresponding economic conditions of life and a political constitution suited to them. These were precisely the things the struggle then under way in Germany was trying to achieve.
For the absolute governments and their following of parsons, professors, country squires, and officials, it provided a welcome scarecrow to ward off the threatening bourgeoisie.
It offered a sweet aftertaste to the bitter pills of flogging and bullets that these same governments were then administering to Germany’s working-class uprisings.

While “True” Socialism thus supplied governments with a weapon against the German bourgeoisie, it also directly represented a reactionary interest: that of the German Philistines. In Germany the _petty bourgeois_ class, a _relic_ of the sixteenth century that has kept reappearing in different forms ever since, is the real social foundation of the existing order.

Preserving this class means preserving Germany’s existing order. The bourgeoisie’s industrial and political supremacy threatens it with certain destruction, through the concentration of capital on one side and the rise of a revolutionary proletariat on the other. “True” Socialism seemed to kill both birds with one stone. It spread with the speed of an epidemic.

A robe woven from speculative cobwebs, embroidered with rhetorical flowers and soaked in the dew of sickly sentiment: this was the transcendental garment in which the German Socialists wrapped their pitiful, skin-and-bone “eternal truths.” It worked wonders for their sales among such a public. German Socialism, for its part, increasingly recognised its vocation as the pompous spokesman of the petty-bourgeois Philistine.

It declared Germany the model nation and the German petty Philistine the representative human being. Every vile, mean trait of this model man received a secret, elevated, Socialist interpretation—the precise opposite of its real character. It went so far as to oppose outright Communism’s “brutally destructive” tendency, proclaiming its lofty, impartial contempt for every class struggle. With very few exceptions, the so-called Socialist and Communist publications now circulating in Germany, in 1847, all belong to this foul and enfeebling literature.
2. CONSERVATIVE, OR BOURGEOIS, SOCIALISM
One section of the bourgeoisie wants to remedy social grievances so that bourgeois society can continue to exist securely.

This section includes economists, philanthropists, humanitarians, people seeking to improve working-class conditions, organisers of charity, members of societies against cruelty to animals, temperance fanatics, and backroom reformers of every imaginable sort. Moreover, this kind of Socialism has been elaborated into fully developed systems.
Proudhon’s _Philosophie de la Misère_ may serve as an example of this kind of Socialism.

The Socialist bourgeois want every advantage of modern social conditions without the struggles and dangers those conditions necessarily produce. They want society as it stands, stripped of its revolutionary and disintegrating elements. They want a bourgeoisie without a proletariat. Naturally, the bourgeoisie considers the world it dominates the best of all worlds. Bourgeois Socialism turns this comforting belief into various more or less complete systems. It demands that the proletariat put such a system into practice and thereby march directly into the social New Jerusalem. What it actually demands is simply that the proletariat stay within the confines of existing society while abandoning all its hateful ideas about the bourgeoisie.

A second version of this Socialism, more practical but less systematic, tried to discredit every revolutionary movement in working-class eyes. It argued that mere political reform could bring workers no benefit; only changes in the material conditions of life, in economic relations, could do that. By such changes, however, it certainly did not mean abolishing bourgeois relations of production, something only a revolution could achieve. It meant administrative reforms that left those relations in place. Such reforms therefore leave the relationship between capital and labour entirely untouched; at best they cut the expense and simplify the administrative tasks of bourgeois government.
Bourgeois Socialism finds its proper expression only when it has become nothing more than a figure of speech.

Free trade—for the working class’s benefit. Protective duties—for the working class’s benefit. Prison Reform—for the working class’s benefit. This is bourgeois Socialism’s final word, and the only word it means seriously.
It comes down to this phrase: the bourgeois remains a bourgeois—for the working class’s benefit.
3. CRITICAL-UTOPIAN SOCIALISM AND COMMUNISM
We are not speaking here of the literature that has always voiced proletarian demands in every great modern revolution, such as the writings of Babeuf and others.

The proletariat’s first direct attempts to achieve its own aims took place amid universal excitement, as feudal society was being overthrown. They necessarily failed: the proletariat itself was still undeveloped, and the economic conditions for its emancipation did not yet exist. Those conditions still had to be created, and only the approaching bourgeois age could create them. The revolutionary literature accompanying these first proletarian movements therefore necessarily bore a reactionary character. It taught asceticism for everyone and social levelling in its crudest form.

Socialist and Communist systems in the proper sense—those of Saint-Simon, Fourier, Owen, and others—arise in the early, undeveloped stage of the conflict between proletariat and bourgeoisie described above (see Section 1, Bourgeois and Proletarians).

The founders of these systems do see class antagonisms and the workings of the elements dissolving the existing form of society. But to them the proletariat, still in its infancy, appears as a class without any historical initiative or independent political movement of its own.

Because class antagonism develops at the same pace as industry, the economic situation they encounter does not yet provide the material conditions for proletarian emancipation. They therefore look for a new social science and new social laws that will bring those conditions into being.

Historical action is to give way to their own inventive activity; historically developed conditions of emancipation are to give way to imaginary ones; the proletariat’s gradual, spontaneous organisation as a class is to give way to an organisation of society specially devised by these inventors. In their eyes, future history amounts to promoting their social plans and putting them into practice.

In designing their plans, they are aware that they care chiefly for the working class’s interests, since it is the class that suffers most. The proletariat exists for them only in this aspect: as the class suffering more than any other.

The undeveloped class struggle, together with their own surroundings, leads these Socialists to imagine themselves far above all class antagonisms. They want to improve the lot of every member of society, including the most privileged. They therefore habitually appeal to society as a whole, without class distinctions—indeed, they prefer to appeal to the ruling class. For once people understand their system, how could they fail to recognise it as the best possible plan for the best possible society?

They therefore reject every kind of political action, especially revolutionary action. They want to reach their goals peacefully, preparing the way for the new social Gospel through small experiments, necessarily doomed to fail, and through the force of their example.

These imaginary pictures of a future society are painted while the proletariat remains very undeveloped and has only an imaginary conception of its own position. They correspond to that class’s first instinctive longings for a general reconstruction of society.

Yet these Socialist and Communist publications also contain a critical element. They attack every principle of the existing society, and so are full of exceptionally valuable material for educating the working class. Their practical proposals include abolishing the distinction between town and country, abolishing the family, ending industries run for private individuals’ benefit, and ending the wage system; proclaiming social harmony; and reducing the State’s functions to the mere supervision of production. All these measures point solely towards the disappearance of class antagonisms. At that time those antagonisms were only just emerging, and the publications recognised them only in their earliest, blurred, undefined forms. For that reason these proposals are purely Utopian in character.

The importance of Critical-Utopian Socialism and Communism declines as historical development advances. As the modern class struggle develops and takes definite form, these imaginary positions outside the struggle, these imaginary attacks upon it, lose all practical value and theoretical justification. Thus, although the creators of these systems were revolutionary in many respects, their followers have invariably become mere reactionary sects. They cling to their teachers’ original views in opposition to the proletariat’s advancing historical development. Consistently, therefore, they try to deaden the class struggle and reconcile class antagonisms. They still dream of experimental social Utopias: isolated “phalansteres,” “Home Colonies,” or a “Little Icaria”—duodecimo editions, tiny volumes, of the New Jerusalem. To bring these castles in the air into existence, they must appeal to bourgeois feelings and purses. Gradually they sink into the category of reactionary conservative Socialists described above, differing only in their more systematic pedantry and their fanatical, superstitious faith in the miraculous powers of their social science.
They therefore fiercely oppose every political action undertaken by the working class. In their view, such action can arise only from blind refusal to believe in the new Gospel.
Thus the Owenites in England oppose the Chartists, while the Fourierists in France oppose the “Réformistes.”

chapters.title: IV. Position of the Communists in Relation to the Various Existing Opposition Parties
paragraphs: Section II explained how the Communists relate to existing working-class parties, including the Chartists in England and the Agrarian Reformers in America.

The Communists struggle to achieve the working class’s immediate aims and secure its interests at the present moment. Yet within the movement of today they also represent and safeguard that movement’s future. In France, they join with the Social-Democrats against both the conservative and the radical bourgeoisie, while retaining the right to criticise the phrases and illusions traditionally passed down from the great Revolution.

In Switzerland, they back the Radicals while remembering that this party contains conflicting elements: partly Democratic Socialists in the French sense of that term, and partly radical members of the bourgeoisie.
In Poland, they back the party that makes an agrarian revolution the first requirement for national emancipation—the party that stirred up the Cracow insurrection in 1846.
In Germany, whenever the bourgeoisie acts in a revolutionary manner, they fight alongside it against absolute monarchy, the feudal squirearchy, and the petty bourgeoisie.

But they never stop, even for an instant, teaching the working class to recognise as clearly as possible the hostile antagonism between bourgeoisie and proletariat. This will enable German workers to turn the social and political conditions that must accompany bourgeois supremacy immediately into weapons against the bourgeoisie. It will also enable the struggle against the bourgeoisie itself to begin as soon as Germany’s reactionary classes have fallen.

The Communists focus chiefly on Germany because it stands on the brink of a bourgeois revolution. That revolution must take place under more advanced conditions of European civilisation, and with a far more developed proletariat, than England’s revolution in the seventeenth century or France’s in the eighteenth. Moreover, Germany’s bourgeois revolution will be only the prelude to a proletarian revolution following immediately upon it.
In short, wherever they are, Communists support every revolutionary movement directed against the existing social and political order.
In every such movement, they put the property question at the forefront as its central issue, whatever stage of development that question has reached at the time.
Finally, wherever they work, they strive to bring the democratic parties of every country into union and agreement.

The Communists scorn any attempt to hide their views or aims. They state openly that their goals can be reached only by forcibly overthrowing all existing social conditions. Let the ruling classes shake at the prospect of a Communist revolution. Proletarians stand to lose only their chains. A whole world is theirs to win.
WORKING MEN IN EVERY COUNTRY, JOIN TOGETHER!
